summary: Chinese has no tenses; instead three small markers show how an action is seen. 了 le after the verb: the action is complete (我买了两张票 ‘I bought two tickets’); 了 at the end of the sentence: something new is the case (他来了 ‘he’s here (now)’, 下雨了 ‘it has started to rain’). 过 guo after the verb: experience, ‘have ever done’ (我去过北京 ‘I have been to Beijing’). 在 / 正在 zài / zhèngzài before the verb: in progress (他在吃饭 ‘he is eating’) — the same 在 as ‘to be at’, so 他在吃饭 is literally ‘he is at eating’. Negation: completed actions are denied with 没 and the 了 disappears (他没来 ‘he didn’t come’); experience keeps 过 (我没去过北京 ‘I have never been to Beijing’). 了 is not a past tense: when you only say WHEN something happened or describe a habit, there is no 了 (昨天我在家, 以前我常常去); a future action can be complete too (明天吃了饭我们走).

rows: 我买了两张票。 I bought two tickets.
他来了！ He’s here! · 下雨了。 It’s raining now.
我去过北京。 I’ve been to Beijing.
他在吃饭。 He is eating.
blocks.caption: Aspect: how the action is seen

items.title: 去了 — went
points: 他去北京了。 He has gone to Beijing (and is there now).

items.title: 去过 — has been
points: 他去过北京。 He has been to Beijing (some time, and came back).

blocks.title: 了 is not a past tense
blocks.text: 昨天我在家 ‘yesterday I was at home’ — no 了: the time word already says ‘past’, and nothing was completed. 以前我常常去公园 ‘I used to go to the park often’ — a habit, no 了. But 明天吃了饭我们走 ‘tomorrow, after we have eaten, we’ll leave’ — a future 了. Think ‘done’, not ‘past’.

blocks.title: 没 swallows 了
blocks.text: 他来了 → 他没来 (never *他没来了). But 过 stays: 我去过 → 我没去过.

blocks.title: Verb-了 likes a number
blocks.text: 我买了两张票 sounds finished. With a bare object, put 了 at the end instead: 我买票了 ‘I’ve bought the tickets’ — 我买了票 alone sounds as if something should follow (…就走了).

items.title: 在 + place (S11)
points: 他在家。 He is at home.
他在家吃饭。 He eats at home.

items.title: 在 + verb (S14)
points: 他在吃饭。 He is eating.
他正在吃饭呢。 He’s eating right now.

blocks.title: The verb never changes
blocks.text: German has no aspect forms and uses gerade for ‘in progress’. Chinese marks aspect with separate particles, and the verb itself never changes: 吃了, 吃过, 在吃.

blocks.title: Questions
blocks.text: 你吃了吗？ ‘have you eaten?’ (also a greeting) · 你去过中国吗？ ‘have you ever been to China?’ · 他来了没有？ ‘has he come or not?’

askYourself: Is the action done and counted (two tickets, three days)? → verb + 了 + number + noun.
Is something new the case now (he’s here, it’s raining, I’m off)? → 了 at the end.
Am I talking about an experience, ‘ever / once’? → verb + 过.
Is it going on right now? → 在 / 正在 + verb (+ 呢).
Is it negative? → 没 + verb, and drop 了; keep 过 (没去过).
Am I only saying WHEN, or describing a habit? → no 了 needed.
Did I put 了 only because the event is in the past? → check: is it complete or new? If not, remove it.
steps: Done → 了 after it (or at the end); ever → 过 after it; going on → 在 before it.
Negate with 没 (drop 了, keep 过).

traps: *我没去北京过 → 我没去过北京 (过 right after the verb).
*昨天我在家了 — no 了 for a plain past state: 昨天我在家.
*以前我常常去了公园 → 以前我常常去公园 (a habit takes no 了).
*他正在到 → 他快到了 (到 cannot be ‘in progress’).
他去过北京 (has been and come back) ≠ 他去北京了 (has gone there).
了 le after a verb ≠ 了 liǎo ‘to finish’ (了解 ‘to understand’).

quiz.why: 没 negates the completed action and 了 disappears; 他不来了 means ‘he isn’t coming any more’.
在 before the verb = in progress.
Completed action with a number: verb + 了 + number + measure word + noun.
Experience negated: 没 + verb + 过.
A plain past state needs no 了 — 昨天 already says when.

quiz.q: 他去北京了 vs 他去过北京:
options: he has gone (is there) vs he has been (some time)
he will go vs he went
quiz.answer: he has gone (is there) vs he has been (some time)
quiz.why: 了 = the going is done and he is away; 过 = an experience in his past.

notes.text: Greek marks aspect inside the verb (έφαγα ‘I ate it’ / έτρωγα ‘I was eating’), and the split is close to 了 vs 在: complete vs ongoing. But Greek always marks tense as well; Chinese marks only aspect, and only when it matters.
Russian aspect pairs (съел / ел) feel like 吃了 / 吃: the perfective ‘done’ ≈ verb + 了. But Russian marks aspect on every verb, Chinese only when it matters — and 了 also works in the future (明天吃了饭我们走).
Spanish comí / comía split complete and ongoing in the past; Chinese 吃了 / 在吃 split them without any tense. estoy comiendo ~ 我在吃; ¿has estado en Pekín? ‘have you ever been’ ~ 你去过北京吗？
The English past tense is not 了: ‘yesterday I was at home’ is 昨天我在家, without 了. ‘I have been to Beijing’ ~ 我去过北京; ‘he is eating’ ~ 他在吃饭; ‘I bought two tickets’ ~ 我买了两张票.
French passé composé / imparfait (j’ai mangé / je mangeais) split complete and ongoing in the past; Chinese 吃了 / 在吃 split them at any time. être en train de ~ 在 / 正在.
German has no aspect forms; ich habe gegessen covers both 吃了 and 吃过. Chinese chooses: 我吃了 (done, now), 我吃过 (ever). gerade ~ 正在.
Hindi marks aspect with participles and auxiliaries: खाया ‘ate (done)’ ~ 吃了, खा रहा है ‘is eating’ ~ 在吃; Chinese uses separate particles and no tense.
Persian mi- marks ongoing or repeated action (mikhordam ‘I was eating’), dāshtan + verb the progressive now (dāram mikhoram ~ 我在吃); Chinese uses 在 before the verb and 了 / 过 after it.
Marathi marks aspect with participles and आहे: खात आहे ‘is eating’ ~ 在吃, खाल्ले ‘ate’ ~ 吃了; Chinese uses separate particles and no tense.
Arabic perfect and imperfect (akala / yaʾkulu) mix aspect with tense; Chinese separates them: 了 says ‘done’, a time word says ‘when’.
Modern Hebrew has tenses but no aspect forms (akhalti ‘I ate’ covers 吃了 and 吃过); Chinese has no tenses but marks aspect: 吃了, 吃过, 在吃.
Turkish -iyor ‘in progress’ ~ 在 / 正在 and -di ‘done’ ~ 了 are suffixes on the verb; Chinese uses separate words and adds no tense.
Japanese 食べた ‘ate’ ~ 吃了, 食べている ‘is eating’ ~ 在吃, 食べたことがある ‘have eaten (ever)’ ~ 吃过 — the same distinctions, made with verb endings.
Korean 먹었어요 ‘ate’ ~ 吃了, 먹고 있어요 ‘is eating’ ~ 在吃, 먹은 적이 있어요 ‘have eaten (ever)’ ~ 吃过 — the same distinctions, made with endings.
Finnish shows completion with the object case: luin kirjan ‘I read the book (through)’ vs luin kirjaa ‘I was reading the book’; Chinese marks it on the verb with 了.
Hungarian preverbs often mark completion (megettem ‘I ate it up’ vs ettem ‘I ate, I was eating’); Chinese uses 了 after the verb: 我吃了.
Swahili -me- ‘has done’ (nimekula ‘I have eaten’) ~ 了 and -na- ‘now, ongoing’ ~ 在 are prefixes on the verb; Chinese uses separate particles and no tense.
Luganda marks tense and aspect with affixes on the verb; Chinese marks only aspect, with separate particles (了, 过, 在), and the verb never changes.
Vietnamese uses the same kind of particles: đang ~ 在 (ongoing), rồi ~ 了 (done, a new state), từng ~ 过 (ever), đã for completed or past: tôi ăn rồi ~ 我吃了.
Inuktitut marks time and aspect with suffixes inside the verb word (nirilauqtunga ‘I ate’); Chinese adds separate particles to an unchanged verb: 我吃了.

seeAlso.note: German has tenses but no aspect: ich habe gegessen / ich aß for the past, gerade or am Essen sein for ‘in progress’; Chinese has no tense but three aspect markers (了, 过, 在) on an unchanging verb.
Arabic’s perfect (فَعَلَ) and imperfect (يَفْعَلُ) are close to a completed / ongoing split, but they are built into the verb and also carry tense; Chinese adds 了 or 在 to the bare verb.
Modern Hebrew has past, present and future but no aspect marking: אָכַלְתִּי ‘I ate / I have eaten’; Chinese distinguishes 吃了 (done) and 吃过 (ever eaten) where Hebrew does not.
没 (S08) is the negation of completed and experienced actions: 没来, 没去过.
